findings.title: Denial-cache test does not actually prove the short-circuit
findings.body: The new sub-test "Should deny on explicit cache deny entry" seeds the permission cache with `map[string]bool{"dashboards:uid:dash1": false}` while the comment claims "Allow access to the dashboard to prove this is not checked". A value of `false` means `checkPermission` would deny anyway, and the fallback path uses the default `fakeStore` (no permissions), which also denies. The assertion `assert.False(t, resp.Allowed)` therefore passes whether or not the new `permDenialCache` short-circuit at the top of `Check` works. To actually cover the new behaviour the scope map must grant access (`"dashboards:uid:dash1": true`) so that the test fails if the denial cache is ignored. Additionally there is no test asserting that `permDenialCache` is written after a DB-confirmed denial (service.go:153-155), so that half of the new logic is untested.

findings.title: Every non-allowed Check now hits the database; denial cache is per (name, folder) and unbounded
findings.body: The cache lookups were removed from `getUserPermissions`/`getAnonymousPermissions`, and `Check` now falls through to `getIdentityPermissions` (a real `permissionStore.GetUserPermissions` query) whenever the cached scope map does not already allow the request. The only protection against repeated queries is `permDenialCache`, whose key includes the resource name and parent folder (cache.go:30) and whose TTL is only 30s. Consequently a caller that checks many distinct resource names the subject cannot access (object-by-object checks, or a client enumerating names) produces one uncached DB permission query per unique (action, name, folder) tuple, and fills the shared local cache with one entry per tuple (the authlib local cache has no size bound), so both DB load and memory are driven by caller-controlled input. This amplification is worse in-proc because the client-side cache was also disabled (rbac.go:103). Consider keeping a bounded/short-lived "permissions were just fetched" marker per (user, action) so the full re-query happens at most once per short interval rather than once per resource.

findings.title: Denial cache key built from unescaped '_'-joined fields can collide
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` concatenates `action`, `name` and `parent` with `_` separators and no escaping, so distinct requests can produce the same key: e.g. name="a_b", parent="" and name="a", parent="b_" both yield `...<action>_a_b_`. Dashboard/folder UIDs may legally contain underscores and are user-chosen, so a crafted (or merely unlucky) pair of UIDs makes a cached denial for one resource deny access to an unrelated resource for up to the 30s TTL (availability/incorrect-deny, not escalation, since only denials are stored). The key also omits group/resource, relying on `action` to encode them. Use a separator that cannot appear in UIDs/actions or include explicit length/field delimiters.

findings.title: Stale folder tree still causes denials, and those denials are now cached
findings.body: `Check` now re-queries permissions from the DB when the cached scope map does not allow the request, but `checkInheritedPermissions` -> `buildFolderTree` still returns the cached folder tree (30s TTL) and is never refreshed when the requested parent folder is absent from it. So for a resource whose access is granted only through inheritance from an ancestor (e.g. a dashboard created in a brand-new subfolder of a folder the user has permissions on), the tree does not yet contain the new folder, the check denies, and the denial is then stored in `permDenialCache` (line 154), extending the window during which the user cannot see the newly created object. The stated goal of the PR (immediate access to newly created folders/dashboards) is therefore only met for directly-granted scopes. Consider re-fetching the folder tree (or at least not caching the denial) when `req.ParentFolder` is not present in the cached tree.

findings.title: permissionCacheUsage metric is mislabelled on the new Check paths
findings.body: In `Check`, a denial-cache hit increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="true"}` (line 118) even though the permission cache was not consulted at all, conflating two different caches in one metric. Conversely, when the permission cache *is* hit but the result is "not allowed", execution continues and line 137 increments `permissionCacheUsage{hit="false"}`, reporting a cache miss for a request that was served from the cache. Cache hit-rate dashboards/alerts built on this metric will be wrong after this change; the denial cache should get its own metric and the hit label should reflect whether `getCachedIdentityPermissions` succeeded.

findings.title: Denial cache keyed on raw subject UID instead of the resolved user UID
findings.body: `permDenialKey` uses `checkReq.UserUID`, the raw value parsed from the subject, while `permCache` keys use the resolved `userIdentifiers.UID` (see `getCachedIdentityPermissions`/`getUserPermissions`). Because `GetUserIdentifiers` treats a numeric subject as a user ID, the same identity addressed as `user:1` and as `user:<uid>` gets two independent denial entries (wasted lookups/queries), and a user whose UID is literally a decimal number shares denial entries with the user whose internal ID equals that number, which can deny the wrong identity for the TTL. Resolve the identifiers first and build the denial key from `userIdentifiers.UID` for consistency.
